m.t: A Treasure in Jars of Clay
o: Heavenly Father, I thank you for the gift of this morning. You woke me with life, with breath, and with the chance to begin again. Before the noise of the day reaches me, I want to pause a moment before you and acknowledge that everything I am and everything I have comes from your generous hand.

Lord, you know how fragile I am. You know my limits, my weariness, and my hidden fears. Today I do not want to pretend to a strength I do not have. I want to remember that you have entrusted a treasure to me in a jar of clay, so that it may be seen that the power comes from you and not from me. Teach me to live simply, without seeking the places of honor, and to treat with affection those who seem small in the eyes of the world.

Guide my words, my steps, and my decisions. Help me to listen before speaking, to serve before demanding, and to smile even if no one thanks me for it. Place in my path people who need a kind word, and give me a heart willing to offer it. When this day is over, may I be able to say that I walked with you, with humility and with peace. Watch over my family, my friends, and all who carry burdens today that I cannot see. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 25, 1881, Angelo Roncalli was born in Sotto il Monte, a small village near Bergamo in northern Italy. His family were sharecroppers, peasants who worked land that was not their own and lived with only the bare necessities. There were thirteen brothers and sisters, and the household held together through the work of all, shared prayers, and a simple faith passed down from parents to children.

Nothing in that home suggested the boy would go far. But Angelo felt a desire to serve God very early on. He studied for the priesthood, was ordained in 1904, and for many years carried out quiet assignments, far from the headlines. He served in various countries, and those who knew him remembered his warm manner, his good humor, and the way he listened to each person as if they were the most important one.

Already advanced in age, he was elected bishop of Rome in 1958 and took the name John XXIII. Many thought he would be a transitional pope, an elderly man who would barely keep things as they were. Yet a few months later he announced that he was calling a great council, hoping that the Church would speak to the world with clarity and closeness. He died on June 3, 1963, and many still remember him as a kindly shepherd.

Roncalli's story needs no embellishment. It reminds us that God often works with people of humble origin, who do not seem important and do not think themselves important. It is the same truth the apostle Paul wrote: we carry the treasure of the Gospel in jars of clay. What is precious is not the jar, but what God has placed in it.
m.c: May the Lord fill your day with serenity and good cheer. Walk simply today, knowing that God sustains what seems small and fragile. His grace is sufficient for you, and his company will not fail you at any moment of this day.
m: Today I want to talk to you about something we sometimes forget: your worth does not depend on the apparent greatness of your life. Paul wrote to the Corinthians that we have this treasure in jars of clay. A clay jar is ordinary, it can break, and it impresses no one. Yet God decided to put in it what is most precious: his light and his love.

This changes the way we begin the day. If you feel small, tired, or poorly prepared, you are not disqualified. On the contrary, you are right where God's strength shows most clearly. He does not look for perfect jars; he looks for available ones. The life of Angelo Roncalli, born into a peasant family, shows us that simplicity is no obstacle to God using us.

Paul also advised the Romans not to be proud in their thinking, but to be drawn to what is lowly, and not to be wise in their own eyes. It is very practical advice. Someone you live with needs you today to treat them as an equal. It might be a coworker whom almost no one greets, an elderly neighbor, a child who asks too many questions, or a relative who feels forgotten.

Here are three steps for today. First, as you begin, say to God sincerely: Lord, I am made of earth, but I am yours. Second, look around you for a simple person and give them real time, without watching the clock or your phone. Third, when something succeeds, give the credit to God and to those who helped you. That way the treasure will keep shining, and the clay will stay in its place, serving with joy.

o: Lord Jesus, as night falls, I come to you with a grateful heart. Thank you for this day, for the bread on the table, for the people who surrounded me, and for every moment when I felt your hand on my life. Even in the hard hours you were near, and today I want to acknowledge it with humility.

Like Nicodemus, I come to you by night, with questions and weariness. There are things I have not understood, decisions that still weigh on me, and matters I could not settle. I bring no answers; I bring only what I have. I give you my doubts, my hurry, and my worries for the people I love. You know what I cannot put into words, and so I rest, knowing you understand me better than I understand myself.

Thank you, because you loved the world so much that you gave your Son, and because you did not send him to condemn but to save. This truth gives me peace. Forgive what I did wrong today and what I failed to do. Keep my home, my family, and those who sleep far from me. Give me peaceful sleep and a waking with renewed hope. I place in your hands everything that remains unresolved, trusting in your kindness. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: The Gospel of John tells us there was a man named Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews. He was a respected teacher, knowledgeable in the Scriptures, with a position to protect. Yet something in the words and works of Jesus troubled him. He had questions he could not resolve from his teacher's chair, and he decided to seek out Jesus in person.

John points out an important detail: Nicodemus came to Jesus by night. Perhaps he wanted to talk without the pressure of the crowd, or perhaps he feared what his colleagues would say. Whatever the reason, he was sincere. He told Jesus that they knew he had come from God as a teacher, for no one could do the signs he did unless God was with him.

Jesus did not send him away or criticize him for coming in secret. He welcomed him and spoke to him about being born again, a deep change that only God can work in the heart. Nicodemus did not understand everything at that moment, and he said so frankly. The conversation contained the best-known words in the Bible: that God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.

Nicodemus's story does not end that night. Later we see him defending Jesus with caution before the Pharisees, and finally helping with his burial. That nighttime visit was the beginning of a light that grew little by little. That is why it encourages us: no one comes to Jesus seeing everything clearly, and the night is no obstacle to meeting him.
t.c: As you close this day, hand over to the Father what you could not settle, and accept his quiet embrace. He keeps watch while you sleep, and his love is greater than any worry. Rest, for tomorrow his mercy will rise with you.
m: There are hours of the day when questions weigh more heavily, and night is often one of them. When everything falls silent, the unfinished matters, the conversations we replay in our minds, and the fears without a name come to the surface. Nicodemus knew that feeling well. That is why he went to find Jesus by night, and found in him an open door.

The first thing this story teaches is that you do not have to put your thoughts in order before approaching God. Nicodemus arrived with questions and left with a seed of faith. You too can come with your doubts just as they are. God is not scandalized by a clumsy prayer, a weary silence, or a heart that does not yet understand.

The second is that God's love is the greatest answer to anxiety. John reminds us that God sent his Son not to condemn the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. If God did this for you, you can trust that he will also care for your family, your work, and your future. What you did not settle today is not a sign of abandonment.

As a practice for tonight, do three simple things. Write on a piece of paper the worries running through your head and hand them over to God out loud. Give thanks for three concrete things that happened today, however small. Then read John 3:16 slowly and stay for a moment in silence. Lie down knowing that the light of Christ does not go out when night falls.
